# Over-the-air upgrading for enhancing security of intelligent connected vehicles: a survey

## Abstract

The continuous improvement in the connectivity, automation and autonomy levels of Intelligent Connected Vehicles (ICVs) significantly increases the probability of potential security threats. Over-the-Air (OTA) is a promising technique for upgrading features of ICVs and enhancing their reliability and security against environmental disturbances as well as malicious attacks. To better understand the potential security risks and possible countermeasures, we survey research works in ICV security during OTA from cloud upgrade, terminal upgrade, and object upgrade. We also summarize existing methods in OTA upgrading techniques and systematically investigate the overall framework of OTA upgrading methods from the perspectives of Software-Over-the-Air (SOTA) and Firmware-Over-the-Air (FOTA).We further discuss possible mitigation strategies and open issues yet to be resolved in this research direction. This survey shows that OTA provides a powerful technique for upgrading the ICV features and improving ICV security.

## 1 Introduction

With the continuous development of wireless communication technology, vehicles are developing towards networked and Intelligent Connected Vehicles (ICVs) in the foreseeable future (Chai et al. 2024; Almehdhar et al. 2024; Ušinskis et al. 2024; 4; Yang et al. 2024). While the ultimate goal of modern ICVs is to design an Internet of Vehicle (IoV) system with high reliability and security, the continuous increase in system complexity and improvement in the automation and connectivity levels of ICVs significantly increases the probability of potential functional flaws and security vulnerabilities (Zhou et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2021; Xiong and Qi 2022; Hao et al. 2021; Yang et al. 2024; Shirvani et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2023). The online upgrade function is an efficient and cost-effective mechanism for fixing these bugs and releasing new features for enhancing reliability and security.

Unfortunately, as demonstrated by existing research works (Luo et al. 2023; Nwakanma et al. 2023; Huang et al. 2023; Wang 2024; Zhang et al. 2024; Lauser et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024), the upgrade mechanism itself can raise security risks. There have been numerous research efforts towards a secure upgrade process. However, most of them focus on the security of individual cloud upgrade, network upgrade or terminal upgrade, while the security of the entire cloud-network-terminal upgrade for an ICV system is still an open research problem. Recently, Over-the-Air (OTA) has emerged for its significance in upgrading the entire cloud-network-terminal, which maintains and enhances the functionality and robustness of the entire ICV system (Sun et al. 2021; Mugarza et al. 2021).

OTA upgrade techniques play a vital role in ICVs, making them smarter and more secure (Halder et al. 2020; Kornaros et al. 2020; Lopes et al. 2020; Otoum and Nayak 2021; Ghosal et al. 2022; Yeasmin and Haque 2021; Malik et al. 2022; Nasr et al. 2022). It improves the functionality, performance and security of ICVs and can also be used for fault diagnostics and troubleshooting. The vehicle OTA upgrade covers nearly all major vehicle modules, including the vehicle power control, infotainment networking, security control, chassis electronic, body control and auto drive systems. In addition, the update process is reversible and fail-safe, allowing for quick error recovery. Overall, OTA ensures timely and reliable updates for ICVs (Sahin and Yang 2022; Hu et al. 2022; Wang et al. 2022; Shi et al. 2022; Li et al. 2022).

However, due to the exposure of many external interfaces (e.g., On-Board Diagnostics (OBD), Universal Serial Bus (USB), and Auxiliary (AUX)) during an OTA upgrade process, it can bring about unknown security threats. For example, as the potential vulnerabilities in the OTA upgrade system or insecure software verification processes, malicious firmware may be transmitted to the vehicles. As a consequence, attackers may inject malicious code into the Vehicle Control Unit (VCU) through an OTA update channel, thereby stealing sensitive information or interfering with the control integrity of vehicles.

This work makes some efforts towards a secure OTA upgrade process by systematically reviewing numerous research works in the ICV security during OTA upgrading. It investigates the security risks against OTA, systematically summarizes the mainstream OTA methods, and discusses possible mitigation strategies as well as open issues that need to be resolved. Our efforts would benefit research in online ICV upgrade and its security.

### 1.1 Survey contribution

The current ICV security reviews mainly consider network security (Checkoway et al. 2011; Wang et al. 2019; Dibaei et al. 2020; Chen et al. 2023), physical security (Luo et al. 2020; Chen 2023), privacy protection (Landini 2019; Yu and Cai 2022; Cai and Yu 2024), software security (Halder et al. 2019; Sharmin et al. 2023; Hu et al. 2024), and regulatory compliance (Bonanti 2020; Shevchenko 2019, 2022; Li et al. 2023), etc. Table 1 summarizes the representative research works in the field of ICV security. There is lack of a systematic study on OTA upgrading techniques, a critical component of ICV security. Moreover, existing reviews on ICV security during OTA upgrading technology have limitations in terms of scope or tend to require upgrading to reflect the latest developments in the field (Kexun et al. 2020; Nidamanuri et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022; Gao et al. 2023).

Therefore, this survey aims to demonstrate how the OTA upgrade technique can help prevent security risks, enhance defense capabilities, and promote in-depth development of related research and understanding. These measures are crucial for updating features of cloud-network-terminal of ICVs, and also helpful for maintaining the reliability and security of ICVs. The motivation behind this survey is to address the significant gap in systematic studies of OTA upgrading techniques in ICV security, aiming to develop a comprehensive framework that not only mitigates security risks, enhances defense capabilities but also advances theoretical insights for practical applications across cloud-network-terminal systems, thereby paving the way towards more reliable and secure ICVs in real-world scenarios.

This survey presents a systematic view of ICV security by conducting the first comprehensive analysis of OTA upgrading techniques. Compared to previous reviews that are limited in scope and depth, this research aims to fill the gaps by investigating how OTA upgrades can significantly enhance security defenses, reduce risks, and advance understanding in the field. The survey uniquely covers the entire OTA upgrade process, including clouds, terminals and object upgrades. It proposes new research directions to bolster ICV security through novel Software-Over-the-Air (SOTA) and Firmware-Over-the-Air (FOTA) methodologies. This pioneer work sets the stage for future advancements in the reliability and security research of ICVs. Note that we present the first comprehensive survey that focuses on ICV security during the entire process of OTA upgrading.

This survey mainly makes the following contributions:

- Revealing the security challenges encountered by ICVs.
- Summarizing the recent mainstream OTA methods for enhancing ICV security from the perspectives of SOTA and FOTA.
- Performing a comprehensive survey of ICV security during OTA upgrading, including cloud upgrade, terminal upgrade and object upgrade.
- Proposing challenges and potential research directions for ICV security from prevention and protection.

### 1.2 Survey structure

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. In Sect. 2, we introduce the ICV security challenges covering the relevant policies and security problems. Section 3 reviews mainstream OTA upgrade methods for improving ICV security based on OTA. Sections 4, 5 and 6 survey existing works on OTA upgrade respectively, covering both upgrade frameworks and upgrade strategies. We discuss potential research vectors and challenges in Sect. 7 and conclude the article in Sect. 8. Figure 1 shows the overall framework and organization of this article.

## 2 Security challenges of ICVs

In this section, we investigate relevant policies and regulations of ICV security in section 2.1 and introduce ICV security problems in section 2.2.

### 2.1 Policies and regulations

With the rapid growth of global population and car ownership, various policies and regulations have been introduced around the world to ensure the security of vehicles (Fang et al. 2020; Newbolt et al. 2023; Yu and Chou 2022). Table 2 summaries the security regulations and policies regarding ICVs of different countries, which is of significant academic and practical value for researching on the networking, intelligence, and electrification of ICVs. Before 2020, ICV was in the stage of autonomous driving 3.0 (DoT 2018; Anany and Grumert 2019; Maurice 2019; Jacobo et al. 2019; Lei 2019; Dawn 2019). In 2020, the US Department of Transportation released the Auto Drive System 4.0 Yang and Fisher (2021), while the Federal Communications Commission shifted the 5.850G \(\sim\) 5.925G frequency band allocated to Dedicated Short Range Communication (DSRC) to Wi-Fi and Cellular-Vehicle to Everything (C-V2X) technology in the same year Rayamajhi et al. (2020). In 2020, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released a notice to accelerate 5 G development and coordinate with the IoV Hui (2020). The same year, the State Council issued the New Energy Vehicle Industry Development Plan (2021-2035), which seeks to accelerate the formulation of the C-V2X standard Xiangguo (2020). All the security policies and regulations related to ICV mentioned above, as well as research on ICV networking, intelligence, and electrification, have significant academic and practical value.

### 2.2 Security problems of ICVs

As the increasing number of information exchange and open interface expose among ICVs and the outside world, the ICVs have higher levels of automation, allowing vehicles to take over all driving functions Chen and Englund (2016); Buinevich et al. (2021); Wu et al. (2022). And the resulting security issues have also emerged one after another Li et al. (2023); Luo et al. (2023); Nwakanma et al. (2023); Huang et al. (2023); Rico et al. (2021); Wang and Zhang (2022); Chen and Englund (2016); Constantin (2018); Weise (2018); Wouters et al. (2019, 2021); Csikor et al. (2022); Joo et al. (2020); Ghanem and Altawy (2022); Antonioli and Payer (2022), which may cause information leakage of vehicle owners, vehicles out of control, etc. For example, Miller et al. achieved attacks on target vehicles with both wired physical access and wireless remote access, which attacked the engine and steering functions of Jeep Cherokee Valasek and Miller (2015). Another famous case is that the Keen Security Lab of Tencent successfully implemented remote attacks on Tesla Model S/X in 2016 Lab (2016) and 2017 TV (2017); Tencent (2017).
